naeb7w: We have three proposals for the avenue: keep it as it is, reserve a lane for buses, or close it to traffic on weekends. Each participant must explain what problem their option solves and what difficulty they acknowledge, without limiting themselves to defending their immediate interest.
10p6v8e: I prefer to start with weekends. I'm worried about the delivery of goods, and it's not so clear that a permanent lane will improve sales. Even so, I acknowledge that the current sidewalks are narrow and that many people avoid walking here.
31hwbf: I defend the permanent lane with a six-month trial. The bus loses time precisely when the most people are traveling. If we only change the weekends, we won't test that effect. That said, we would have to reserve loading zones and measure access from other neighborhoods.
1athp68: We have a fictional survey of one hundred responses: forty people arrive on foot, thirty by bus, twenty by car, and ten some other way. It was collected on the avenue on a Saturday. How far can we use these data to decide about weekdays?
yqtgxn: They are useful for formulating questions, not for describing the whole week. Maybe more families come walking on Saturdays. I would ask to repeat the observation at various times and talk to businesses that receive large packages. I don't want to turn an impression of mine into a general rule.

1q8ki8s: A city you can live in: a text to interpret
11wbxt: Original SpanishCue material; the situations and data are for teaching purposes, not real news or official exam texts.
1lz8k5g: Turning an avenue into a corridor with more buses and less parking has divided the neighborhood. Businesses fear losing customers; pedestrian associations hope to gain space; those who live far away ask how they will get there if transit frequency does not improve. The discussion tends to be reduced to a choice between cars and people, a formula that works well for a poster but is not enough for designing a policy. Within each group there are different needs, and the same person may walk, drive, and use the bus on different days.
w1nu6r: My proposal is to reserve a lane for public transit and widen the sidewalks through a six-month trial. The measure should be accompanied by loading zones with clear schedules and an evaluation of access from outlying neighborhoods. There is no doubt that space is limited; it is not so clear that keeping all the current parking spaces is the fairest way to share it out. A vehicle parked for eight hours takes up a public resource that other people only need for a few minutes to get around.
11rm1ro: The business objection deserves attention. Some businesses depend on frequent deliveries or on customers with reduced mobility. That said, it does not follow that any reduction in parking will necessarily lower sales. We would have to compare data from before and after, distinguish types of business, and see whether shopping hours change. A voluntary survey on social media can offer experiences, but on its own it does not represent all the people who use the avenue.
t13nzt: The trial should be open to modification. If access time from the periphery increases steadily, connections would have to be strengthened before expanding the project. If sales fall, it would be necessary to study the causes and not attribute every change to the lane. In short, defending a more livable city requires more than a shared intention: it requires public criteria for assessing results and a willingness to correct a decision without turning every adjustment into a political defeat.

I propose expanding the observation before the change and publishing indicators of travel time, accessibility, and commercial activity. I defend a reviewable trial: modifying it on the basis of results would be a sign of responsibility, not a defeat for the project.
